v.why: Pushing an already strong L2 penalty higher causes underfitting and sharp accuracy drops (e.g. 0.129 to 1 lost 5-12 points).
Relaxing an over-strong L2 penalty recovers capacity, giving large gains from alpha=1 and 0.129.
Learning rates near 0.1-1 with Adam diverge or stall, so going higher collapses accuracy.
Reducing an excessively high learning rate restores stable training, with gains up to +36 points.
Very small learning rates leave the network undertrained within 243 epochs, so a larger step helps.
Narrow networks are capacity limited, so adding units helps more than when already wide.
Adding a second layer to a single-layer network adds expressiveness, whereas the edit is less useful from depth 2.
Removing a layer from a 3-layer net tends to reduce capacity and accuracy relative to removing it from shallower nets.
Tiny batches give noisy gradients with Adam, so a modestly larger batch stabilizes training.
Shrinking an already tiny batch increases gradient noise and instability.

raw:
These ten hypotheses come from reading the 100 experiments together with general expectations about MLP training. I didn't run any further analysis. Several (depth and batch size especially) rest on weak or mixed evidence, so treat them as less certain than the learning-rate and alpha ones.

- **Alpha:** the strongest evidence is at the high end. Raising alpha from 0.129 to 1 cost 5 to 12 points on all three datasets (#9). Lowering alpha from 1 gave +6 to +14 (#11).
- **Learning rate:** edits at the high end were consistent. Going down from 0.0774, 0.278 or 1 was mostly positive (#71–73), and going up from 0.278 was strongly negative (#69). At the low end, going up was mostly positive (#61, #62).
- **Width:** growing a narrow network tended to help (#81, #85, #90). #86 is a counterexample, but it also had a high learning rate.
- **Depth and batch size:** the evidence is thinner. Adding a layer to a one-layer network was positive in #45 but mixed elsewhere. Removing a layer from a three-layer network was mostly negative or mixed (#53, #55, #60). A larger batch at tiny sizes looked positive (#21, #22), and a smaller one looked negative (#38).
